item.title: Revel in Charleston Nightlife at These Bars and Restaurants
item.description: Charleston is known for its colorful façades, its wondrous oaks and palmettos, and music flowing from its alleyways. item.title: The VinePair Podcast: Has Hospitality and Etiquette Within the Trade Fallen Apart?
item.description: There’s always been clear, unspoken etiquette for hospitality workers: Order simple drinks, don’t hound bartenders during a busy service, don’t expect a comped tab, and tip well. item.title: The Jack Daniel’s Age-Stated Releases Are a Hit, but How Old Can the Tennessee Whiskey Get?
item.description: When it comes to high-end whiskey, Jack Daniel’s is on a roll. (Or perhaps more appropriately, a heater, based on the ABV of some high-octane releases.) From toasted barrel whiskey to “hazmat” rye, the famed Tennessee distillery has staked its claim among top producers of premium spirits. Those efforts have helped expand the brand beyond the Old No. 7 bottle, an omnipresent SKU that keeps it among the top two biggest sellers of American whiskey. item.title: The World’s Best Riesling Regions, Mapped
item.description: Riesling is a profoundly aromatic grape used to create several distinct styles of wine. It’s also one of the most popular white wine grapes in the world. Native to Germany, the grape is exceptionally durable, with relatively thick skin that allows it to thrive in cool climates and develop its signature acidity. item.title: Ask a Somm: Does Wine Really Need to Rest After Traveling?
item.description: While some drinkers purchase their wine at bars, restaurants, and liquor stores, others anxiously await the arrival of a case at their doorsteps. Tourists order bottles to their homes after traveling to winemaking regions, wine clubs ship cases to subscribers, and another sector of consumers purchase theirs from the vineyards themselves. item.description: It seems that each day brings a new headline about younger generations’ drinking slump, but the doom and gloom offers American wine the opportunity to reinvent its old ways to meet the desires of contemporary drinkers. Now is a pivotal time for the U.S. wine scene, but it’s up to the producers to speak with consumers and adapt to their changing demands.
